title: Holiday wishes from the Hubble Space Telescope
caption: The spiral galaxy M74, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: M74, Phantom Galaxy · constellation Pisces · about 25 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage (STScI/AURA)-ESA/Hubble Collaboration

recognition.text: Ranked #42 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Bright pink patches are sprinkled along the spiral arms in this Hubble view of M74, a spiral galaxy about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Pisces, also known as the Phantom Galaxy.

Each pink patch is a huge cloud of hydrogen gas. Hot young stars embedded inside give off strong radiation that strips electrons from the hydrogen atoms, and the ionised gas glows in response. Astronomers call these star-forming regions HII regions, a label for hydrogen that has lost its electrons. They also show an excess of ultraviolet light, another sign of the hot stars inside.

HII regions make useful signposts. Because the clouds are relatively short-lived and are lit by young stars, they mark the places where a galaxy is forming stars in the present era rather than in the distant past. Following the pink patches along M74's arms is a way of tracing where its newest generations of stars are coming into being.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.34 x 3.22 arcminutes) and distance (25 million light years), the frame spans roughly 24,000 × 23,000 light-years. Its light set out about 25 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters; the full colour mapping isn't published, though the glowing hydrogen appears pink.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye can, and the near-infrared filter records light we cannot see.
